title: Training Large Models on Limited GPUs

content.title: Training Large Models on Limited GPUs

blocks.text: Training large models on limited GPUs is the practical, hands on problem every technique in this module has been building toward, combining quantization, LoRA, and several complementary memory saving tricks together to fit a fine-tuning run into hardware that would otherwise be completely insufficient.

This closing topic of the LoRA and QLoRA module pulls those pieces together into one practical playbook, and covers a few additional techniques, gradient checkpointing and gradient accumulation, that stack alongside QLoRA for even tighter memory budgets.
1. The Core Constraint, GPU Memory

blocks.alt: Model size against the GPU memory limit determines whether it fits

blocks.text: The fundamental question every fine-tuning project on limited hardware faces is simple to state, does the model, plus everything needed to train it, gradients, optimizer state, activations, actually fit within the available GPU memory, and every technique covered in this module exists to push that answer from no toward yes.
2. Combining QLoRA Techniques Together

blocks.alt: Quantization, LoRA, and gradient checkpointing together let a model fit on a limited GPU

blocks.text: The core QLoRA recipe combines 4-bit NF4 quantization of the frozen base model, covered in the earlier topics of this module, with LoRA training on top, and stacking gradient checkpointing on top of that combination pushes memory savings even further for especially constrained hardware.
3. Gradient Checkpointing as a Complementary Technique

blocks.alt: Storing all activations is compared against recomputing them as needed

blocks.text: Normally, a forward pass stores every intermediate activation needed to compute gradients later during backpropagation, consuming significant memory. Gradient checkpointing instead discards most of these intermediate activations and recomputes them on demand during the backward pass, trading additional compute time for a substantial memory reduction.

code.content:
# Enabling gradient checkpointing, conceptually
model.gradient_checkpointing_enable()
# Trades some training speed for meaningfully lower memory usage

blocks.text: 4. Reducing Batch Size and Using Gradient Accumulation

blocks.alt: A small batch size combined with accumulated gradients produces an effective larger batch

blocks.text: A smaller batch size directly reduces memory usage per training step, but can hurt training stability if made too small. Gradient accumulation lets a team use a small physical batch size while still getting the training dynamics of a larger effective batch, by accumulating gradients across several small steps before actually updating the weights.

blocks.text: 5. Choosing a Smaller Base Model When Necessary

blocks.alt: A large base model is compared against a smaller base model

blocks.text: Even after applying every memory saving technique covered in this module, some models are simply too large for certain hardware, in which case choosing a genuinely smaller base model, and accepting a somewhat lower capability ceiling, covered in the earlier discussion of pretraining setting a ceiling on fine-tuning outcomes, may be the most practical path forward.
6. Monitoring Memory Usage During Training

blocks.alt: A training run with memory monitoring gives an early warning before a crash

blocks.text: Actively watching GPU memory usage throughout a training run, rather than only discovering a problem when the run crashes with an out of memory error, lets a team catch a creeping memory issue early and adjust configuration before losing significant training progress.

blocks.title: This mirrors the disk space monitoring discipline used throughout this course content authoring process itself
blocks.content: Checking a resource constraint proactively, rather than reacting only after it fails outright, is a pattern worth applying to GPU memory just as much as to any other constrained system resource.

blocks.text: 7. What to Do When You Still Run Out of Memory

If a training run still exceeds available memory after quantization, LoRA, and gradient checkpointing are all already in place, the remaining options are reducing batch size further, reducing the LoRA rank covered earlier in this module, reducing sequence length, or accepting that the current hardware genuinely cannot handle the current model size.
8. A Realistic Budget Example

A 7 billion parameter model at full 32-bit precision needs roughly 28 gigabytes just for weights, well beyond many consumer GPUs. Quantized to 4-bit with NF4 and double quantization, the base model shrinks to a few gigabytes, and adding LoRA training and gradient checkpointing on top brings the total memory need within reach of a single consumer GPU with as little as 8 to 16 gigabytes, exactly the combination that makes fine-tuning accessible on modest hardware.
9. When Cloud GPUs Become the Practical Answer

blocks.alt: Genuinely insufficient local hardware points toward cloud GPUs, otherwise keep optimizing locally

blocks.text: When a task genuinely requires a model or training configuration too large even after every technique in this module has been applied, renting cloud GPU capacity for the duration of the training run, covered further in the Training Infrastructure module later in this course, becomes the practical answer rather than continuing to squeeze diminishing returns out of local hardware.
Worked Example

A developer with a single consumer GPU wants to fine-tune a 7 billion parameter model, far beyond what full precision fine-tuning could ever fit on that hardware. Combining 4-bit NF4 quantization of the frozen base with LoRA training, double quantization, and gradient checkpointing, they successfully fit the entire training run within their available memory.

When an early attempt still runs slightly over budget, they reduce their LoRA rank from 32 down to 16 and enable gradient accumulation to keep their effective batch size stable, finally fitting comfortably within their hardware constraints while still producing a meaningfully improved fine-tuned model.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting full precision fine-tuning on limited hardware without first considering QLoRA style memory saving techniques
Only discovering a memory problem when training crashes, rather than monitoring usage proactively throughout the run
Reducing batch size for memory savings without adding gradient accumulation to preserve training stability
Continuing to squeeze local hardware indefinitely rather than recognizing when cloud GPU capacity is genuinely the more practical answer

blocks.text: Practice

For a model size and a piece of hardware you have access to or are considering, work through the combination of techniques from this module, quantization, LoRA rank, gradient checkpointing, that would most plausibly let that model fit and train successfully on that hardware.
Key Takeaway

Training large models on limited GPUs comes down to stacking complementary memory saving techniques together, NF4 quantization of the frozen base, LoRA training on top, gradient checkpointing, and gradient accumulation, and knowing how to combine and tune them, along with recognizing when local hardware has genuinely reached its limit, is what turns fine-tuning a large model from impossible into practical on modest hardware.
